title: DL Darius Robinson Press Conference 07-07-26 | Arizona Cardinals 2026
text: Darius, what's kind of the the ramp up like the kind of that in between period between the end of mini camp and then you kind of have this time off now knowing you're only a few weeks away from training camp. What's what's kind of the the ramp up like for you? >> Uh I'd say just get swole. Honestly, just live, run, be in really good shape. Um yeah, just keep working out cuz you know we'll be back in a couple weeks and then it's non-stop. So just make sure you're going in at a place you want to be at. >> What have been your impressions of the new coaching staff, coach Mike Pease? >> Yeah, uh it's been awesome. Uh definitely hearing his philosophies and how he sees the game and thinks about it. Very simple, just be violent, play fast. Uh it's exciting, especially my new D-line coach PK. Uh I definitely like his uh mindset and what he thinks about everything. So I'm excited. >> What is it about his mindset that you like? >> He's just very like like very particular about like the order and how we do our drills, but understanding like why we're doing it and what we're trying to get out of it. And then also it's just like uh we got this new sled and we'll be trying to knock like knock the bolts off of it and it's just super competitive. So it's just um it's awesome and I'm glad he's here. >> What are some of the benefits of having Nick Rallis sticking around? >> I mean it's everything cuz I don't have to really think too much now. Like I feel like it's my third year in our defense, so like like during OTAs I didn't really think about anything. I just played and I feel like that's going to be a big help for me this year. And just familiarity with the calls and everything, so I'm excited. >> Is this year a reset for you personally or is it do you take it as something a lot bigger than that like it's a proving year for you? >> Yeah, no. I just year three. This my third year in the NFL. I'm super excited for the opportunity. Uh I'm just excited to see how I can grow from my first two years, but I'm just excited. It's It's been a lot of different adversities we've had to face, but I'm really excited for this year. >> Do you put any extra pressure on yourself though knowing that it is year three and that you now have, you know, a lot of NFL experience kind of under your belt? >> Not really. I mean, it's football. I mean, that's the way I have to think about it mentally. It's just football. It's just playing a game. You're grinding. You're just getting better and just put one foot forward each day. I feel like if you overthink it, then that's where you get all this pressure and stuff, but no, I'm excited. >> What are you expecting out of yourself this year then? >> Man, I'm expecting to be just a good teammate. Uh be somebody that can be accountable each and every day and really just let the tape do the talking. Like I really don't want to put any goals or things out there. Like just watch the tape and I'm excited to see what I can put on there. >> There were times at the end of last season where you were hard on yourself about maybe not meeting goals that you would set for yourself and then being a first round draft pick. Was there any part of your process this off season that you changed to take that next level in year three from that? >> Yeah, definitely just watching the tape with a magnifying glass and realize like, "Okay, I'm still not getting this or it's still not the level where it needs to be at." So, working more pass rush in the off season, using my hands, like all those different things to help me get the results I want. But it's all the things that I can learn and grow from and look in the mirror and be like, "Okay, I know I can do this, you know? Now I just do put in the effort and time to do it." So, that's why I'm super excited for this year. >> What's the confidence level like to be able to get the results that you do want? >> Super high cuz I know I can do it. It's just can you be consistent? Can you impact the game, impact the team? So, I like putting that on myself though cuz I've played at Missouri five years. I got better and better each year in college. So, that's the same way I envision it now in the league and just having that mindset of just attacking and just one day at a time. So, I'm super excited. >> Is getting in the backfield going to be a the primary thing for you this year? >> I mean, yeah, definitely. Any way you can I know for me like I got to pass rush better, affect the quarterback, get some sacks, like do all that cool stuff, but really just focusing on the small things. Focus on my get-off, focus on my hands, my pad level, and all that stuff, and that'll take care of like what I want to reach for myself. >> You guys had a little turnover in your position group. You bring back Roy Lopez, but what are your expectations for that that room? And and how does it help you do your job? >> Yeah, I think we're all hungry. I think from the past year or two like it just really hasn't been the results we've wanted, and everybody knows in football it starts up front with the D-line. So, I think everybody understands like kind of like the target and what we're willing to do to reach where we want to be. And we got a lot of guys that are super motivated, super hungry, and just super excited for this year. >> What's the biggest thing you can take away from Calais' time here? >> Yeah. Um It's a lot. I mean, he taught me so much, honestly. But really just I think about Calais, I think about like when we was after practice like just going through his pass rush and what he thought, and I'm like, Calais is almost 40 and he's out here every day after practice working on his own craft, but also working to help me get better. So, I would really say that like just time and just reps and and now he meant a lot to me, so definitely going to take a lot of advice he gave to me, you know. >> You going to do this till you're 40? >> Man, I hope I can, you know. Just take it one day at a time, but now Calais, he's a different specimen cuz I used to joke around I was like, man, like I missed more games my rookie year than probably you missed your whole career. And I was like, it's kind of crazy, but I mean, it's the reality of the situation, so just try to get as much advice I can from him. >> What's the chemistry like in that D-line >> Yeah, I think everybody's super close, especially with Roy coming back, you know, cuz Roy was with me in my rookie year. Glad he came back, but then it's kind of like the core like Dante, LJ, Roy. Like I hope I'm not forgetting anybody, but like it's these are the guys that came in with my rookie year. So, it's like I think everybody's hungry. Everybody understands like what we need to do to get done and is willing to do it. So, we're close group. >> Have you seen How have you seen Jonah kind of mesh with you guys? >> Yeah, Jonah, he's really good. Jonah is uh works really hard in the weight room. Um he was with the Saints and he was telling us like similar techniques that they played and how he played it and what he thought about it. So, definitely learning from him a lot. And uh he's a really good player. >> What did you mean last year after week 13 when you said, "I I I'm not who I thought I was." >> Uh you talking about the Tampa game? >> Tampa. What happened? >> Yeah, yeah. That was tough cuz I mean, we didn't win a game in I don't know how long and I feel like really good players, really good players think about like how can I affect the game and win the game for my team? And I obviously didn't do enough cuz we didn't win any games during that time. So, I just put it on myself cuz I know I can be better and I know who I am, but that was more of a thing of realizing like accountability. And I feel like the more times you can have accountability, the more better actions you're going to get out of it. And still we didn't win no games, but uh individually I know I definitely made strides as the season went along and also like heading into my third year is just knowing, "Okay, what am I good at? What am I not good at?" What I'm not good at, I got to pour into that bucket as fast as I can. And what I'm good at, keep pouring as well so I can be the player that I want to be to help this team. So, now I'm just super confident and just accountable of everything. So, it'll be a fun year. >> Your life projections don't have the team with that many wins right now. How motivating is that to see? >> Um honestly, I haven't looked at it. I mean, we won three games, so it's like but you know, you know, so I don't really don't think too much of it, but I know what it felt like all those days we lost, it was miserable. So, you don't want to feel like that next year, so you're going to find a way to not feel like that. So, just super motivated. >> Do you feel like through that adversity that it did kind of become clearer to you how you can make it down and down more consistently in that >> Yeah, facts. Just don't think, just play. And that's something I feel like going to year three like I'm not thinking about anything anymore like I'm just align like JG, uh he used to say all the time alignment, assignment, key technique. And like literally that's the only thing going through my mind each play and just play and just have fun. Honestly, having fun is half the battle like when everybody's all tensed up and stressed about stuff, you're not playing fun, you're not playing fast. So, just make sure you have that on your mind. >> You and that coach connect at all from both being from Michigan? >> Yeah, he was telling me uh he was um from up there and I was like it's a small world. He asked me how I went to Missouri. I was like I was uh I only played my junior year of senior high school, so Michigan was super big at the time and then Michigan State was kind of iffy. So, but now I'm glad he's here, real Michigan guy. >> I know in the past you've done the Sack Summit in Vegas. Are you going back this year? >> Uh I'm not sure yet. Uh I'm just trying to think about um kind of my off season program right now, but it's definitely it was a great experience those first two years seeing all those guys and learning. But yeah, I'll figure it out soon. >> I know BJ's one of the guys that's confirmed to be going there. I know he's done it in the past, too. But like what with those sort of events that the guys like conduct during the off season, just how beneficial are they actually come, you know, by the time you guys get to training camp? >> Yeah, I think it's super beneficial cuz they have like the best players be there and they'll tell you like what was they thinking on their rush moves and what's their mindset like they'll share information like nobody's really gatekeeping. So I feel like as long as you can listen and think okay how can I apply this to my game and stuff like that. So now it's super beneficial. >> Harris, thank you. >> All right, thank you guys. >> Yep.

title: Lamar Jackson's 38 TD Season Is Coming
text: Yeah, there you go. >> go back to the AFC Championship game, the touchdown that that Zay caught that came off of Lamar having to, you know, get turned around in the pocket. So, he definitely has that as part of his repertoire. No doubt about it. It's just who's going to be that next guy to step up. And then you the interesting point that you make and one thing I'll give Eric DeCosta credit for is really went out and stacked. Like there's there's so many paths that the Ravens wide receiver room has to generating those kind of two key play playmakers that they need. Like is it going to be Serratt as a big slot? Is it going to be James Proche? Is it going to be Taysir Mack? Is it going to be We know what Zay is going to do. I have no doubt about that. And then, you know, going back to what Jeff said on the show last week, he's hearing a lot of positive buzz about what he's seeing from or what they're seeing in practice from Le'Jonte Wester. He's kind of become, you know, the guy taking the backseat to all these flashy new toys and we have to remember, you know, he's going to be in that competition as well probably as, you know, the backup slot guy, the the returner. But what can he get you, you know, after after some of the explosive plays he put on tape at the University of Colorado. So, it's just interesting. There's so many paths that could shake out whereas I don't think I've ever felt this confident with some of the mid-round wide receivers that the Ravens have drafted in the past. Like guys like Jordan Lasley and chucking the ball into the lake and you know, some of some of those some of those some of those names of the past. And I'm just really intrigued at what could shake out. I think this is probably the most excited I've been from a questionable wide receiver room if that makes sense. Just Like let's be real. These They're they're question marks until, you know, Bateman's going to be a question mark until he gets back to form. Taysir is a question mark until he can consistently make those big plays on Sundays. The rookies are always question marks and that's no disrespect to them. It's just until they do it at the NFL level, doesn't matter. So, there's a lot of question marks, but I think a lot of excitement for a lot of them. I think the preseason's going to be really fun cuz it's going to be one of those positions where I think these guys are going to get a lot of run. Zay and Bateman probably won't, but I think you're going to see a lot of the rookies through the preseason games, which is awesome from a film perspective. Great content for me. I love it. So, I'm looking forward to that. >> [laughter] >> Yeah, let me let me add one more thing, Bobby, real quick. I feel so good about that and what they've done with the offensive line and Coach Ledford and where Derrick is and where Lamar is that we've seen uh way less talented offensive rooms than this and the Ravens have a number one seed because the offensive line and Lamar got work done with and and we had this and this is when it was running back by committee to some degree. You know what I mean? It wasn't Derrick Henry. So, when I think about the bread and butter of what we do, under center, outside zone, everything kind of, you know, play action running off of that, and then looking at Zay, I think Mark is going to have a Pro Bowl type season. I believe he's going to have a re-emergence. I've been saying this for a long time. I just seen guys being considered dead and gone and because of how serious they take their craft and how important it is to them and then being healthy and having a new coach a new offensive line coach and a new coordinator, they kind of get reinvigorated and before you know it you're like, "Oh, we thought he was done." But now he's back to 2024 or 2023 numbers. So, yeah, I'll pause there, but that those are my thoughts too on top of >> I I love the Mark prediction because if there's one thing we know about Mark and it sucks, right? Because he's a guy that I wish everyone could kind of rally behind because of what his mindset is. He's one of those guys that he cares an awful lot about the game he plays. He's very He's just one of those guys that, you know, he goes into the building every day and is one of the hardest workers. And I feel like that's the kind of mindset that leads to a really good bounce-back story. So, I think that's like that prediction I love and I would love to see. Plus, good-looking fella. Got to give him >> Oh, there's been only a couple comparisons over your time in the content space for your team. Um, [laughter] and while the [clears throat] receiving yards has taken a dip since the hip drop tackle and that gruesome ankle injury, the touchdowns, the red zone production, right, his rapport with Lamar hasn't. And I think that's what Femi is banking on here coming back in the form of of this re-emergence that he speaks of. Uh, you may have just answered this, Femi, and I know you're getting up against the clock here, so we'll let you go here soon. You may have just answered this, but just to confirm, and this is this will be a projection, but as you look at the '26 season, this time next year, are they still, the Ravens, going to be considered a run-first group offensively entering '27? >> I think they're [laughter] always going to be a run-first group. I I just think it's the way business is done in the AFC North, um, and the teams that matter, like Kansas City, which I think is going to have a re- resurgence as well, Buffalo, you got to be able to run the ball, you know? So, um, you know, I I made a prediction today. I had them as a top-10 passing offense, a top-three run offense, and a top-five scoring offense. You know, I made this prediction. I have Lamar at 38 passing touchdowns, six or seven rushing, 400 4,200 passing yards, uh, 38 passing touchdowns and eight interceptions was my prediction for Lamar. I have Zay with 1,400 yards and seven receiving touchdowns. You know what I mean? So, uh, success begets success. And what I mean by that is when your defense is good, you get more possessions on offense. When you get more possessions on offense and you score, you get more possessions on offense. You know what I'm saying? So, I just think it it just feeds itself. So, the numbers that I'm saying aren't even like record-breaking numbers for Lamar. Now, maybe the passing yards are, but the rest of them aren't. I expect Lamar to rush for 600 yards probably. Um zone read is going to be less used than it ever has. Lamar is going to need to get his run yards when the pocket breaks down and he sees run lanes. Remember, there's been plenty of times over the years where Lamar has had room to run and he's chosen not to for whatever reason. Now, sometimes those turn into big passing plays. I want Lamar to get 7 or 8 yards a bounce. He's so good at that. Just go ahead and do that. Cuz when you start doing that, Lamar, I mean as if he's listening to us, right? I'm talking to Lamar directly right now. When he starts taking advantage of those open run lanes, it forces the defense to adjust and make changes. You know what I mean? Like, oh wow, he is he is running more. Now, he starts running more, then what happens? Guys get behind the defense again and then you just kind of cycle your way in and out based on what the defense gives you. So, yeah. So, Bobby, I'm I'm I'm really excited about what this offense is going to be, but I do not think they're going to be the Rams. I I don't I and I think it would be a mistake to become the Rams. I I don't think that's that's not who we are. Now, in any given week, could we have a game where we decide, okay, if Lamar is going to throw for 350 and we're going to rush for 100, okay, so be it. You know what I mean? That's fine. That's what you need to do to win that week. But when it's all said and done, they're going to be a top three rushing offense as as as we usually tend to be and I think that's the way business needs to get done and I think it's the best and most direct way to a Super Bowl. >> It reminds me of how cyclical the NFL is because the talk, if we go back to like 2018, 2020, 2021, all all the talk was about the shift to more spread concepts and the NFL getting more pass-heavy and you know, we're we're not going to see the run game. It's going to turn into the CFL where maybe you see 10 rush attempts a game and now you're starting to see it things are getting heavier, things are getting more physical again. It's less about speed, it's all about the run game and it just it it always makes me chuckle just to see how cyclical it is and it makes sense, right? As as you start to build out something, what's that counter punch? When you have your jab, where's your hook? And you got to keep developing that. And that's why it always comes down to you need to be able to do everything. Like that is what good football teams do. When the Ravens have won Super Bowls, their teams have been able to run the ball, pass the ball, stop the run, stop the pass. You you you you if you're excellent at those four areas, you're going to be a good football team. You're going to contend. And then it really comes down to capitalizing in clutch moments. And that is ironically what has prevented this this iteration of the Ravens era. Um they haven't been able to capitalize in those clutch moments. That's what's held this team back despite statistically being usually great efficiently in those four areas of the game. >> Well, you know what's interesting too, Fem? Like Sure, is it a small sample size offense considered? Yes. But in replacing Isaiah Likely, like we all know they have to do effectively at the tight end position. And they've tried to do that already with these players that we're talking about in Quevoss and Hebner. And then of course retaining Mark Andrews and bringing in Durham Smythe to do some of the Ricard dirty work. They're going to have to replace the clutch gene that Isaiah Likely gave them. Because you could make an argument that in recent seasons, he may have been outside of Lamar who yeah, hasn't stacked a full game if you will in the post season, a signature game if you will. He's had signature moments. He's had signature halves. He's had signature stretches of time in in January. Isaiah Likely was right there with him. >> Yeah, I I think that a lot Isaiah is given a lot of grace because of all the big plays he's made. Correct me if I'm wrong here. I mean, we know that Mark had a fumble and he dropped a two-point conversion. I think Isaiah Likely had a fumble in that game, too, if I'm not incorrect.

title: How Texans built out role for 'confident' Woody Marks
text: Hey guys, Aaron Wilson. One of the watershed changes surrounding the Texans new look offense has been the addition of veteran running back David Montgomery. And adding the man they call Knuckles as their new RB1 obviously changes the calculus for the other running backs, especially Woody Marks. He goes from the Texans featured back as a rookie after he overtook Nick Chubb as the primary back to now he's in a complementary role. And it's one he embraces. It's not like he's fought this change at all and he has really taken to his new role and it's looked pretty smooth so far. So he's dropped some pounds. He's down to about 212 lb and he did this by design to be lighter, to be more flexible, and to be more suited to pass catching duties. So when you're thinking about fantasy football and about a flex back, think about Woody Marks. And he's also going to be a kickoff returner. So they have him involved in more than one facet of the game. So not only is he going to be doing a lot for Danny Barrett, the Texans running backs coach and assistant head coach, and Nick Caserio, the offense coordinator, and of course Cole Popovich, the offensive line coach and run game coordinator, but he'll also be involved in Frank Ross, special teams coordinator's return units. So I think that that's well suited for what Woody does well. One of the most prolific pass catching backs in recent college history, not just at USC, but in his Southeastern Conference days at Mississippi State. And I can tell you I've been watching him catch the football for a while now. Remember the 50-yard reception against the Baltimore Ravens? He's more than capable of having a lot of production, eluding linebackers and defensive backs in the open field. He has vision, he has some wiggle, he's got some moves, and his speed is deceptive. When he gets out there and he's free in the open field, I don't see people catching him. I see him running away from guys, eluding pursuit, and making people miss. So, he has all the qualities to be an outstanding third down back. And it helps they've got Darren Sproles here on a Bill Walsh coaching fellowship to not only help him with kickoff returns, along with Jaylen Noel, their primary punt returner, but also to talk to him about third down back duties. People forget Darren Sproles was a very formal running back for the Chargers, and then later the Eagles. But, what I saw from Woody last season, had a real defined ability to adapt on the fly. He would elude tacklers in tight spaces. He would create yards out of nothing. He had enough power to break some tackles. Wasn't the biggest back. He held onto the football. The fumble in the AFC divisional round game, very uncharacteristic of Woody. And although a bit underutilized compared to his college days, very adept at catching passes out of the backfield. He was also a bruising pass blocker. And that's one of the things that's gotten a lot of praise from the coaching staff is how he can protect quarterback C.J. Stroud. So, he was a starting running back for a playoff squad. And after replacing Chubb as the centerpiece of this up-and-down running game, he was patient. And he was a big part of the 10-game winning streak. He was the back that had 703 yards, leading the team in rushing last season. Not a giant number, but still respectable for a rookie. Had a couple of touchdown runs. Caught 24 passes for 208 yards and three touchdowns out of the backfield. And now in this complimentary role, what the vision is, they have a solid workload for Marks. So, in talking with Danny Barrett, we'll hear from Danny in a minute, big thing is he feels like Woody understands his role, and he'll get a lot of opportunities. That's a quote. A lot of opportunities. So, last year they kind of brought him along slower. Now, they see him playing faster. They like what he can do on special teams. And this is something that's also drawn praise from Frank Ross. And Frank Ross is not someone that just throws around praise lightly. So, when you get that from Frank, you earned it. And Woody has earned it. And I've spent time with Woody this off season before and after the Montgomery addition. He knew they would bring in another back. So, we were having these conversations going back to time when he made a school appearance and I had an exclusive with him to when I talked to him in the studio, to when I've had a Zoom with him, and to a lesser extent just talking casually at his bowling event. And Woody and David have become quick friends. And David has mentored him. They've hung out together. David supported his bowling event, which is for charity for his foundation to help underprivileged kids in Atlanta and Houston. And the big thing with Woody, you know, the Steelers game jumps out to me. That's when it counts. It's a wild card playoff game. It's in the cold. And he rushes for a season high 112 yards and a touchdown. And I know no one played well against the Patriots, including Woody and especially C.J. Stroud. He gets 17 rushing yards on 14 carries. There was nowhere to go. They were just completely stonewalled. They had 48 yards on the ground. And that's one of the biggest reasons that David Montgomery is here to revitalize a running game that was just running on neutral most of the season. But let's look closer at what Woody did. Was there a lot of holes to run through? Did they have run blockers like Wyatt Teller, the new Pro Bowl guard they've plugged in at left guard? Did they have Keelan Rutledge, the guy they call Big Red, a first-round draft pick? And Ingram, you could count on him for run blocking, but you couldn't always count on it from some of the other players. Titus Howard, better in pass blocking often than run blocking. I thought that they got a jolt in the arm from Trent Brown, but it was a lot of injuries surrounding the offensive line. Ariyon Tureaud got better as the season went on. I think that he has a lot of upside as a run blocker, but you look at what they're doing and Nick Caserio's plan for him, and we'll get into that right after this break. title: Defensive Line Interviews | Giants Huddle | New York Giants
text: We're back here. Another edition of the Giants podcast brought to you by Citizens official Bank of the Giants. Our player interview series continues. We head over to the defensive side of the ball. And defensive tackle is a position that has had a lot of turnover over the past six months. A lot of new faces, some veteran players, some really young players, a good mix, a good group, a fun group of guys to talk to. Here's my conversation with them. All right. Now, we're joined by Giants edge rusher Tony Coulson. Tranty, how are you, man? >> I'm blessed. What you said? >> Good. So, how do you fit into this scheme? Are you going to be on the edge more? Are we going to see a little bit of three tech the way they're using you? How do you feel your usage is going to be if you want to give that up or if you want to be a little innocuous about it and get that too? >> I guess we'll we'll see when the cards are shown. >> Fair enough. [laughter] The one thing I've noticed though is that they like to be big at a lot of these positions, right? And I feel like just if you look at the size of the guys, like your edge group is pretty big and you kind of fit in with with with with that group of guys pretty well based on just your frame and stature, right? >> Mhm. Yeah, we got some some pretty big guys. I'm the tallest and the heaviest. Unfortunately, [laughter] >> unfortunat I'm not sure if that's unfortunately. Honestly, Harbaugh probably likes that to be honest. >> I like that. I like it. We have a lot of versatility in the room. Multiple like we all have big guys, but everyone is playing to their strengths and some are big with speed, some are big with a lot of power, some are very twitchy and bendy. You know, I like it. >> Does this scheme remind you of anything that you've done in your past? Um, uh, this scheme has a lot of different pieces that I've seen from other schemes. So, that's nice. Like a lot of >> I can't Yeah, just a lot of other things I've seen. >> Why do you think it's a good scheme for you? Uh, I think it's a good scheme for everyone because there are multiple plays to where if this isn't your play style, then this play can help you or this this form this grouping is like fit more to this type of person and cater to others and other uh personnel. So, it's I like it. It's very multiple. >> It allows you guys to use the way someone described to me is that they have non-negotiables. you have to be able to do this, but they almost let you achieve those goals based on how you're able to succeed, right? >> Yes. Yes. That's Who said that? That's perfect. Actually, [laughter] I don't know who said that, but kudos to him. Like, that's a very good way of putting it >> as a player. Is Is that what you're looking for? >> Yeah. You want You want to be able to use what makes you special while also fitting within the scheme. And that like what makes you special isn't like looked at as a bad thing. Some places it's like, okay, you can do what you can do. You're either going to do what we say or >> they focus on what you can't do rather than what you can do. >> And it's like, okay, I can't do that. But you want you want to harp on that. Like, let's harp on the things that I do great and let's build something around that. >> What is it about Dinard Wilson as a coach at a guy that that makes him a fun defensive coordinator to play for? Um, first of all, like he if he see bull he calls bull and I like that. Like as a player, you can like if you if someone keeps it real with you, you want you want someone to keep it real. You don't want someone that's going to lie to you and he's going to call it like how he sees it and he has a very high threshold of what he likes and we're all raising to that level and we're trying to exceed that. So I like that. >> I like it. All right. Uh, finally, where are you trying to make a jump this year? Obviously, last year must have been a little frustrating for you. A lot of injuries. Um, what do you want to show this year that you weren't able to do last year because of all that? >> That I can be healthy. [laughter] >> Uh, you know, you got to start with that first and [clears throat] then, you know, uh, put together a healthy season and build off what I've done in the past. >> All right. Now, we welcome in one of the newer members of the Giants on the defensive side of the ball, defensive tackle DJ Reer. DJ, how are you, man? >> I'm doing pretty good. How about you? >> I'm doing great. Uh, so you signed a little bit later in the process. Yeah. Um, what went kind of through that, you know, waiting till when you did and signed to come here when you did? A lot of teams like they try to get through the draft and figure out where they're at. Is that kind of what >> I think that's kind of what happened. I had uh some family things had to take care of on my end and then uh making sure that was all taken care of at home and it was good. And then I think also the process just like kind of waiting till the draft, seeing what you're going to do, seeing what's available and you know I knew I was kind of a priority. So, right after that happened, I wanted to be able to get up here and get things done. >> Why was Yeah, I think we all understand why the Giants would want you. Why Why for you were the Giants the right place for you to land? >> Uh, I think just kind of a similar thing. I think there's we had mutual interest. Uh, some good players around on both sides of the ball and um I think it was going to be kind of a new start no matter where I went. And I felt like this was a fresh start for everybody with some good pieces. Uh, with some really really good pieces. You don't really kind of walk in a locker room and see a lot of players that you see in ours and it seemed like a special place and I've gone against Harbs in the past and kind of seen how he goes about things. I thought I've always respected him as a coach and I was like why not? It seems like a great place to be. >> Between Harbs and then also Dinard Wilson and how they are going to run this defense. Why do you think that was a good fit for your skill set with how they play? >> I think I've just watched the defensive pass in Baltimore and Tennessee. Um just kind of watching him in the past. What up Ben? [laughter] uh watching them in the past and just kind of seeing what they did uh that with the players they had uh looking kind of through the playbooks and just seeing how things would go. I thought it'd be a good defense for me to be in. Um me and Dinard in a couple offseasons before tried to hook up before in Tennessee and try to figure things out. So it end up working out this time and working it way way into fruition. for you as someone that's been part of some really good defenses in the league for a long time stopping the run. What's the key for a team to have a good run defense? >> Uh just building the wall and like really wanting to uh the run comes down to like effort and uh I think this league though every I think everybody outside in this league try to convince you it's a passing league, it's a passing league, it's passing league and yeah it is. A lot of teams do pass the ball and there's a lot I mean numbers are crazier than we've ever seen them but if you can't stop the run teams aren't going to pass the ball like they're they have no reason to and um so I think that's a bigger part of the game and I think the teams who run the ball the best still are the teams who go deeper in the playoffs. I mean I I don't have a exact stat on it but from the way I see it if you're giving up a lot of rush yards your team probably and if you're rushing for a lot of yards your team's going to win. So if you're stopping the run, I think you got a better chance of winning than you do just any other way. >> And you say build the wall. So I imagine then discipline is also a big part of that, right? Correct. Because you know, if you see a potential to make a play in front of you, you try to shoot a gap, you get out of your gap, then all of a sudden everyone else in the defense is screwed because you're not on the spot you got to be. So how important is making sure everyone is gap sound and is disciplined part of that sound run defense? I think it's the hardest thing when you go from uh playing football at every level that like to stay in your I mean you've been making plays your whole life, >> right? >> You've been running around making plays your whole life since you've been a little kid. And I think that's probably one of the harder things transitioning to this league is everybody's good. >> It's not a will the running back find that hole if you do something extra. It's he's going to find it, >> He's going to find that gap. No m anytime I've ever been outside of my gap in this league, the running back's found it. I don't know how he knows that I'm out my gap. he knows. [laughter] And um so it's just one of those things where you have to be disciplined on and trusting those guys out there with you. And that's where those practice reps come in. When I can trust that Tummaine's going to be here or these guys are going to be here and you know they're going to be in their gap so I don't have to do anything extra. If I take care of my knock it back, make it a little bit cleaner pitcher for the guys on the back end. They can come in and fill their gaps and they can get the tackle down. I think that's where practice reps are super important and you start to really trust your brother and you don't end up doing the extra stuff that you did as a little kid when you knew little Johnny beside you just he couldn't make the play and that's okay. You know what I'm saying? He was your boy and you play wreck ball with him and that's how it goes and you had to get over there. So your whole life you've been kind of taught that hey I'm an athlete. I'm out here. I'm supposed to make these plays. But now you're playing with other athletes and you got to trust them to be professionals and do their job as well. Every defensive coordinator likes to describe their defense as being multiple. Yeah, it it's kind of a buzz word in the league. You know that. >> But talking to a different guys on this defense, it seems like that really is the case here, especially up front because I've asked different guys up front like, "Oh, you going to be two gapping? Are you going to be gapping a halfing?" And they're like, "Well, we're kind of going to be doing everything based on the play." >> Yeah, it's a lot. It's a lot in here. Um, but I like it that way. You know, I always think you can add a lot in and then trim it more than trying to have things short and then expand when guys are comfortable in the system. Um, but I think there's just a lot of different fronts. There's a lot of different ways you're showing. I think it's important. It's it's cool to be a a smart player in this defense, but I also think like you get to be you. And I think that's going to be fun for a lot of guys. Like you get to do things not necessarily how you do them. It's just within the schemes of how you do them. Uh maybe you show a little bit different than this guy. Like and that's okay. >> By the way, every player in this defense has said the exact same thing to me. >> Maybe you show a little bit different than this guy and that's okay. Like maybe your stance or what the way you get about things, but your your job is to do this and if you get there and do your job, of course there's a standard way we want to teach to do it, but if you get there, we're not tripping about that. That's the way it went. So it's it's been cool to kind of see everybody go about it different ways. different groups, first team, second team, third team guys all making plays and and and the way they're going about it is fun. >> All right, finally, what do you think about your room? Because I think it's a really unique set. You got like three rookies, uh, Bobby Jameson, Travis, a couple undrafted free agents as well. Then you have some guys that are over 30, have been the league for a long time and done it really well. So, it's like it's a fun combination of vets and and young guys kind of What do you think this room is going to be like? And when all is said and done, we figure out who's going to be on the roster. How is this group going to work together? Do you think >> it's been fun right now because um you know I got um a guy who I play with Josh Tupal. He's a fun guy. I've you know really gotten to know him. AD's that kid's talented. I you know didn't know Toledo just had so many ballers down there. Just just sitting at the school. We got to get these kids >> especially the second Toledto's got everybody now. >> Apparently they got everybody down there. Um you got AD you got the like you said you got the young guys. It's a unique unique setting of a room that I've been in. You got Lucky. Um, so it's it's fun though. It's It's fun, man. And I think it's a good group. I think that that's where your group can really shine. You got somebody kind of in every age gap kind of, you know, us bringing it's taking a little youth from them trying to stay a little bit younger and them trying to mature a little bit, taking some things from us and us being able to talk. And, you know, you got guys in those groups that are hungry and motivated and that's that's what's fun. Um, you got kids chasing contracts, trying to change their lives, and you got like a old guy on me, like me, just trying to hold on, play some good ball, and try to shape these kids and help them, you know, help them as much as possible, cuz I believe in leaving the game better than what you found it. And so, I hope that I can help these kids, and they can help me, and, you know, we can have a really, really good year. I think we got some special talent in there. Coach Johnson's a really, really good coach. So, I'm excited. I'm really excited. >> I'd like one more quick followup. Have you ever played in front of two inside linebackers that look like Tmaine Edmonds and RB? >> Not that tall. Not that big. No. No. I've played and I've had some big like last year I was with uh Alex and then Jack Campbell and those are pretty big guys. But like I haven't >> not this yet. Not Not this big. Just in the middle. I was telling uh one of my friends that yesterday we had a phone call. I said >> I've just never had two linebackers like this big long rangey. >> Those guys could play defensive huge back there. And like, you know, I'm sitting there as a dtackle and like I'm looking up in the huddle. I'm like, man, that's [laughter] crazy just looking around. But yeah, there's some big guys. >> All right. Now, we're joined by a Giants defensive lineman, Lucky Fu. Lucky, what's going on, man? How are you? >> I'm well, man. Thank you. Thank you for having me here. >> What has it been like fitting in here and and trying to learn what all what it's all about to be a uh a Giant? >> Um, I've been taking it in since day one. Um, you know, with the new staff, uh new teammates, but uh so far, you know, uh everything's been smooth. you know, our chemistry building up this uh during this OTAAS, you know, having everyone in the building. Uh, you know, I'm I'm I'm really excited for what we got, uh, building up this year. >> Yeah. But in your room, it's been a lot of moving pieces in there, right? You've had some new guys come in and some of guys have left. What has it been like trying to build chemistry in that room where it's hasn't been a consistent group since day one? >> Shoot. I mean, you know, for me, you know, having a room like this, you know, with the different guys and different, uh, experience levels, um, you know, based off what they had on before, you know, new guys got in. Um, you know, I'm excited with the guys that we got in our room. You know, we got a bunch of hardworking guys, big, tough guys. Um, you know, that's not afraid of taking, uh, up the new task, you know, of what this uh, uh, team is asking for, you know, up front. So, you know, uh I'm I'm excited to be with these guys and and to work towards that goal that we have. >> You're a vet. You had a couple other vets in Shelby Harrison and DJ Reader. What does having those kind of veteran presence in the room? What does that do for a group? Having a set of guys like the three of you that know what you're doing, have kind of been around the block a few times. >> It's It's kind of weird being called a vet now, but um >> You are though. >> Yeah. [laughter] But um you know uh for me you know I I tend to look up to those guys right there. Um you know DJ um you know Shelby you know uh Josh you know coming in new addition. >> Yep. >> Um you know so I tend to try to follow their footsteps still but also you know with our younger guys try to apply you know some of the things that I've learned over the years and um you know hopefully you know we can combine that you know and build this unit up to where it needs to be. >> How have the young guys added to the room? A couple undrafted free agents. You have Bobby Jameson Travis in there as well. How have they kind of tried to fit in with the vet group in that defensive tackle space? >> Oh, man. The the rookies done a good job, you know, so uh so far that I've been here um you know, on and off the field, you know, learning and and trying to you know, uh learn the playbook, trying to uh get this chemistry down with us. Um so, it's it's been nothing but great uh working with these rookies. >> What do you think of the scheme in terms of how how you fit into it and what they're going to be asking you to do within the confines of the scheme up front? Uh I I love the scheme, you know. I think the scheme is, you know, is putting us in the right positions, especially up front. Um you know, to uh you know, that that main goal to stop the run, you know, and that so that can open up, you know, other areas um where that needs to be. But um yeah, with this scheme that uh coach and them got for us, yeah, I'm I'm excited for it. What is it about this system and some of the fundamentals of how how you play up front that you think puts you in good position to try to stop the run like you described? >> Um, I believe, you know, with my role coming here so far, you know, I've been out a little bit more on that end that that fore position where, you know, kind of have more more size outside right there, you know, and obviously we have, you know, some guys inside that can take care of that. So, you know, I think building that wall up front, you know, setting that standard, um, you know, setting that tone up front will, uh, you know, will will set the rest for the back ends. >> You say building that wall, that basically just means making sure you guys are on the same level, right? So, there are no gaps. >> No gaps. No gaps. No, you know, that's that's what we're working on uh, and striving for. >> All right. title: Late Cowboys player Marshawn Kneeland had Stage 1 CTE | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: I received an email today with the press release announcing that Marshaun Neeland, the Cowboys defensive lineman who died at age 24 last year by suicide, and it was a tragedy, and as we have seen in many other cases, the brain of a deceased football player is studied for evidence of CTE. They still don't have a way to diagnose CTE in the living. And in most of these cases, there is some degree of CTE, which isn't a surprise when you're talking about somebody who has played football most of their life. The finding was that Marshaun Neeland had stage one, which is the lowest level. Stage four is the highest. It just underscores the risk. And this goes back to what we discussed last week in the aftermath of the Chris Johnson news that he has ALS. Football players will say, "We know what we signed up for." It's important that they always know exactly what they signed up for. It's not just the injury that can happen to you right now. It is the condition you can develop later in life. And you know, the reality is when you're 23, 25, hell, just pick a number in your 20s. Now, as you get closer to 30, you start thinking about these things more. But the younger you are, you're not thinking about life when you're 60, or 70, 80. It may as well be 500 years away. It's a different lifetime. It's a different person. That guy will worry about it. So, I'd say most players, even if they fully know all risks will still play, especially at the highest levels. But, it's important that they know the risks. We don't want to hide the risks. We don't want to have this moment where, "Hey, everybody knows the risks now." and then time passes and we don't talk about the risks. And that was the reason that Jeff Pearlman was as upset as he was, justifiably so, for the way that the disclosure of Christian Cantwell's ALS was handled with no mention whatsoever. Nothing about the connection between ALS and football, and the connection's real. It wouldn't be one of the conditions that qualify players who retired as of July 7th, 2014 for payment under the NFL's unlimited concussion settlement fund. ALS, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, dementia, CTE. So, it's it's it's not something that we should refuse to talk about because every year there's a new crop of players who are starting to play football. Every year there's another group of college football players. Every year there are college football players who are migrating to the NFL and every year you're going to have people who maybe didn't understand the full risks. Just cuz it's out there doesn't mean they've researched it. They understand the short-term risks. They don't understand the long-term risks and it's fair to talk about it. It's not fair, it's mandatory, I think. Anybody that cares about football, we need to be sure that everyone who's playing fully understands the risk of playing and they accept that risk. They're entitled to accept that risk, but they need to know what it is. That's what the concussion litigation flowed from. The idea that the risk was hidden from them. Now, if that case had gone to trial, plenty of the former players who testified, if telling the truth, they would have said, "I'd have played anyway." But, you still need to know. It's the right thing to do. It's the fair thing to do. It's the responsible thing to do. And it would be irresponsible to just stop talking about it because, "Hey, we all know the risks now." We all know the risks, so let's just act like they aren't there. All right, it's Mike Florio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube.
